q: In which year and city was the English epic poet John Milton born?
e: John Milton was born on 9 December 1608 on Bread Street, Cheapside, London, to John Milton Sr. (a scrivener and composer) and Sara Jeffrey, and died on 8 November 1674.

q: At Christ's College, Cambridge (1625–1632), by what nickname was the fair-complexioned, refined young John Milton known?
e: Milton was nicknamed "The Lady of Christ's" due to his delicate features, long auburn hair, and austere moral habits. He earned his B.A. (1629) and M.A. (1632) from Christ's College.

q: In which year did John Milton become completely blind, inspiring his famous sonnet "When I consider how my light is spent"?
e: Milton lost his sight completely in early 1652 (at age 43) while serving as Latin Secretary (Secretary for Foreign Tongues) to Oliver Cromwell's Council of State (appointed 1649).

q: How many books did the FIRST edition (1667) and the SECOND revised edition (1674) of Milton's 'Paradise Lost' contain respectively?
e: Published in 1667 in 10 books, Milton restructured 'Paradise Lost' into 12 books (matching Virgil's 'Aeneid') in the 1674 second edition by splitting original Books VII and X into two books each.

q: What is the stated central purpose of Milton's 'Paradise Lost' as declared in Book I (line 26)?
o: To "justify the ways of God to men"
e: In the grand invocation to the Heavenly Muse (Urania) in Book I (lines 1–26), Milton prays to illuminate what is dark in him so that he may "assert Eternal Providence, / And justify the ways of God to men."

q: In which verse form is Milton's 'Paradise Lost' written?
e: In his 1668 prefatory note 'The Verse', Milton rejected rhyme as "the invention of a barbarous age" and praised blank verse ("English heroic verse without rhyme") as recovering "ancient liberty" from "the troublesome and modern bondage of rhyming."

q: Milton's famous pastoral elegy 'Lycidas' (1637) mourns the premature death by drowning of which Cambridge college friend?
e: 'Lycidas' (1637, published 1638) laments Edward King, who drowned in the Irish Sea in August 1637. Charles Diodati was mourned separately in Milton's Latin pastoral elegy 'Epitaphium Damonis' (1639).

q: What is the central theme of Milton's celebrated 1644 prose tract 'Areopagitica'?
o: Defence of the freedom of the press against pre-publication licensing
Justification of the execution of King Charles I
Advocacy of divorce on grounds of incompatibility
e: 'Areopagitica' (November 1644) is an impassioned speech to Parliament opposing the Licensing Order of 1643, famously declaring: "as good almost kill a man as kill a good book."

q: 'Comus' (performed at Ludlow Castle in 1634, music by Henry Lawes) belongs to which dramatic literary genre?
e: 'A Masque Presented at Ludlow Castle, 1634' (known as 'Comus') celebrates chastity and virtue through the Lady's resistance to the enchanter Comus, assisted by the Attendant Spirit and the river nymph Sabrina.

q: What do the Italian titles of Milton's famous companion poems 'L'Allegro' and 'Il Penseroso' (c. 1631–32) mean respectively?
o: The Cheerful Man and The Thoughtful/Melancholic Man
e: Written in octosyllabic (iambic/trochaic tetrameter) couplets during his Horton period, 'L'Allegro' invokes Mirth (Euphrosyne) for daytime rural/social joys, while 'Il Penseroso' invokes Melancholy for studious nocturnal contemplation.

q: How many books does Milton's brief epic 'Paradise Regained' (1671) consist of?
e: Published in 1671 together with 'Samson Agonistes', 'Paradise Regained' comprises 4 books (modeled on the Book of Job) depicting Christ's temptation by Satan in the wilderness (Luke 4).

q: In Milton's closet tragedy 'Samson Agonistes' (1671), who is Samson's treacherous Philistine wife who betrayed the secret of his strength?
e: 'Samson Agonistes' (meaning "Samson the Athlete/Wrestler") is modeled on classical Greek tragedy (Sophocles/Euripides) with a Chorus and strict unities. Samson is visited in Gaza prison by his father Manoa, Dalila, and the Philistine giant Harapha.

q: What is the concluding, most famous line of Milton's sonnet "On His Blindness" (Sonnet 19)?
o: "Tomorrow to fresh woods, and pastures new."
"Better to reign in Hell, than serve in Heaven."
"They also serve who only stand and wait."
"Fame is the spur that the clear spirit doth raise."
e: Spoken by personified Patience in the sestet of Sonnet 19 (Petrarchan form: abbaabba cdecde), the final line consoles Milton that humble submission to God's will is itself true service.

q: Who is the fallen archangel who speaks the defiant line "Better to reign in Hell, than serve in Heaven" in Book I of 'Paradise Lost'?
e: Satan utters this defiant boast in Book I (line 263) after awakening on the burning lake of Hell alongside his lieutenant Beelzebub, also declaring "The mind is its own place, and in itself / Can make a Heaven of Hell, a Hell of Heaven."

q: Which magnificent early ode did Milton compose at age 21 on Christmas morning in December 1629?
o: On the Morning of Christ's Nativity
e: 'On the Morning of Christ's Nativity' (1629) celebrates Christ's birth banishing pagan gods and oracles; it marks Milton's first major poetic masterpiece during his Cambridge period.

q: In 'Paradise Lost' Book I, who is the fallen angel architect who builds 'Pandemonium' (the high capital of Satan and his peers in Hell)?
e: Mulciber (the Roman name for Vulcan/Hephaestus, famously thrown from Heaven by Jove to fall from morn to noon to dewy eve onto Lemnos) designs and raises Pandemonium in Book I.

q: In Book II of 'Paradise Lost', which two allegorical guardians sit at the Gates of Hell and unlock them for Satan?
e: Sin (who sprang fully armed from Satan's head in Heaven, echoing Athena from Zeus) and Death (begotten by Satan upon Sin) guard Hell's gates; Sin holds the key and opens the gates into Chaos for Satan.

q: In Books V–VIII of 'Paradise Lost', which "affable Archangel" is sent by God to Eden to warn Adam and narrate the War in Heaven and the Creation?
e: Raphael ("the sociable Spirit") dines with Adam and Eve and narrates Satan's rebellion (Books V–VI) and the six-day Creation (Book VII). Later, in Books XI–XII, Archangel Michael reveals future human history and escorts Adam and Eve out of Eden.

q: In which Book of 'Paradise Lost' does the actual Fall of Man (Eve eating the forbidden fruit of the Tree of Knowledge, followed by Adam) take place?
e: Book IX is the dramatic climax of 'Paradise Lost', where Satan enters the sleeping serpent, tempts Eve (who chose to garden separately from Adam), and Adam eats the fruit out of "fondly overcome with female charm."

q: Which solitary faithful seraph in Book V of 'Paradise Lost' defies Satan in the rebel camp and is praised by God as "Servant of God, well done"?
e: Abdiel ("Among the faithless, faithful only he") stands alone against Lucifer's rebellion in the North of Heaven and flies back to God's throne, becoming Milton's emblem of individual moral courage.

q: Which Miltonic sonnet opens with the fierce invocation "Avenge, O Lord, thy slaughter'd saints, whose bones / Lie scatter'd on the Alpine mountains cold"?
o: On the Late Massacre in Piedmont (Sonnet 18)
e: Sonnet 18 (1655) protests the brutal slaughter of Protestant Waldensians (Vaudois) in Piedmont by troops of the Duke of Savoy; Wordsworth praised Milton's political sonnets ("in his hand / The thing became a trumpet").

q: Who was Milton's second wife (married 1656, died 1658), immortalized in his deeply moving Sonnet 23 ("Methought I saw my late espoused saint")?
e: Milton married three times: (1) Mary Powell (1642, a Royalist's daughter whose brief desertion prompted his Divorce Tracts), (2) Katherine Woodcock (1656–58, celebrated in Sonnet 23), and (3) Elizabeth Minshull (1663).

q: Which 1649 prose pamphlet did Milton publish just two weeks after the execution of King Charles I, defending the right of people to depose and execute a tyrant?
o: The Tenure of Kings and Magistrates
e: 'The Tenure of Kings and Magistrates' (Feb 1649) argued for popular sovereignty and tyrannicide, leading to Milton's appointment as Latin Secretary. 'Eikonoklastes' (Oct 1649) refuted the royalist 'Eikon Basilike'.

q: In 'Lycidas', who is the "Pilot of the Galilean lake" who delivers the stern invective against the corrupt Anglican clergy ("Blind mouths!")?
e: St. Peter (bearing the "two massy keys of metals twain") denounces greedy hireling shepherds ("The hungry sheep look up, and are not fed"), ending with the cryptic warning of the "two-handed engine at the door."

q: In Book II of 'Paradise Lost', during the Great Consult in Pandemonium, which fallen angel argues for "open war" against Heaven?
e: In the Infernal Council (Book II): Moloch urges fierce open war; Belial counsels slothful ease/inaction; Mammon urges building a glittering empire in Hell; and Beelzebub proposes Satan's sly plan to corrupt the newly created Earth and Man.

q: Who famously remarked in 'The Marriage of Heaven and Hell' (1790) that Milton was "of the Devil's party without knowing it"?
e: William Blake argued that Milton wrote "in fetters when he wrote of Angels & God, and at liberty when of Devils & Hell, because he was a true Poet and of the Devil's party without knowing it."

q: During Milton's 'Horton Period' (1632–1638, living at his father's Buckinghamshire estate), which group of poems did he compose?
o: On the Morning of Christ's Nativity only
L'Allegro, Il Penseroso, Comus, and Lycidas
e: Milton's four career periods: (1) Cambridge Period (1625–32: Nativity Ode, On Shakespeare); (2) Horton Period (1632–38: L'Allegro, Il Penseroso, Arcades, Comus, Lycidas); (3) Prose/Political Period (1640–60: Areopagitica, Divorce Tracts, Sonnets); (4) Later Poetic Period (1660–74: Paradise Lost, Paradise Regained, Samson Agonistes).

q: What is the concluding emotional tone and famous final image of 'Paradise Lost' (Book XII, lines 646–649)?
o: Adam and Eve perish in a flood
Angels rebuild the Garden of Eden
Satan is crowned King of Earth
"They hand in hand with wand'ring steps and slow, / Through Eden took their solitary way."
e: Book XII closes with poignant, quiet hope: "The world was all before them, where to choose / Their place of rest, and Providence their guide: / They hand in hand with wand'ring steps and slow, / Through Eden took their solitary way."

q: In 'Samson Agonistes', what famous phrase describes Samson's humiliating captivity in Gaza ("Eyeless in Gaza...")?
o: "Eyeless in Gaza at the mill with slaves"
"Dark, dark, dark, amid the blaze of noon"
e: Line 41 of 'Samson Agonistes' reads "Eyeless in Gaza at the mill with slaves" (later borrowed by Aldous Huxley as the title of his 1936 novel). Line 80 has the equally famous lament "O dark, dark, dark, amid the blaze of noon."

q: To whom did Milton address his 1644 treatise 'Of Education', defining a complete and generous education as one that fits a man to perform "all the offices, both private and public, of peace and war"?
e: Milton addressed 'Of Education' (June 1644) to educational reformer Samuel Hartlib, proposing academies combining classical learning, science, ethics, and physical training.

q: Who coined the famous phrase "Milton's Grand Style" and praised him as the sole English poet possessing "the sure and flawless perfection of rhythm and diction"?
e: Matthew Arnold popularized "the Grand Style" in his essays on Translating Homer and 'Milton' (1888). Key features of Milton's Grand Style include Latinate syntax/inversions, lofty allusions, epic similes, enjambment (verse paragraphs), and sonorous proper names.

q: In Book I of 'Paradise Lost', Milton compares the vast host of fallen angels floating on the burning lake to "autumnal leaves that strow the brooks in Vallombrosa." This is a classic example of:
e: An Epic (Homeric) Simile is an extended, elaborate comparison stretching over several lines, drawing on geography, classical myth, or nature (e.g., Satan's shield compared to the moon viewed through Galileo's "optic glass" from Fiesole).

q: Who wrote the famous sonnet 'London, 1802' opening with the tribute: "Milton! thou shouldst be living at this hour: / England hath need of thee"?
e: William Wordsworth wrote 'London, 1802' praising Milton ("Thy soul was like a Star, and dwelt apart: / Thou hadst a voice whose sound was like the sea"). Tennyson later called Milton "God-gifted organ-voice of England."

q: What is the Latin theological concept 'Felix Culpa' (the Fortunate Fall), expressed by Adam in Book XII of 'Paradise Lost'?
o: The building of the bridge across Chaos
The expulsion of the rebel angels
The paradox that Adam's Fall ultimately brings greater good through Christ's Incarnation and Redemption
e: After Archangel Michael reveals Christ's future sacrifice and redemption of mankind, Adam exclaims (Book XII, 469–478): "O goodness infinite, goodness immense! / That all this good of evil shall produce..." — the classic 'Fortunate Fall' (Felix Culpa).

q: Which fellow poet and M.P. for Hull helped protect Milton from execution after the 1660 Restoration and wrote a commendatory poem for the 1674 edition of 'Paradise Lost'?
e: Andrew Marvell (who had served as Milton's assistant Latin Secretary) intervened in Parliament to secure Milton's release in 1660 and contributed "On Mr. Milton's Paradise Lost" to the 1674 edition.

q: In Book I of 'Paradise Lost', which astronomer — whom Milton had personally visited in Italy in 1638 — is the ONLY contemporary figure mentioned by name ("the Tuscan artist")?
e: Milton visited the blind, house-arrested Galileo at Arcetri near Florence during his 1638–39 Italian tour and refers to him in Book I (line 288, "the Tuscan artist"), Book III (590), and Book V (262, explicitly naming "Galileo").

q: Which critic notoriously attacked Milton's 'Lycidas' in 'Lives of the Poets' (1779) as "easy, vulgar, and therefore disgusting," complaining "Where there is leisure for fiction there is little grief"?
e: Despite calling 'Paradise Lost' "not the greatest of heroic poems, only because it is not the first," Dr. Samuel Johnson disliked the pastoral conventions of 'Lycidas' and Milton's republican politics, also remarking that 'Paradise Lost' "is one of the books which the reader admires and lays down, and forgets to take up again."

q: Who inspired Milton to write 'Paradise Regained' (1671) by famously remarking after reading 'Paradise Lost', "Thou hast said much here of Paradise lost, but what hast thou to say of Paradise found?"
e: Thomas Ellwood, Milton's young Quaker friend and Latin pupil (who found him a cottage at Chalfont St. Giles during the 1665 Great Plague), made this remark in 1665, prompting Milton to write 'Paradise Regained'.

q: In Book IV of 'Paradise Lost', in what animal form is Satan discovered "squat like a toad, close at the ear of Eve," inspiring her troubling dream?
e: Satan first perches like a cormorant on the Tree of Life, then squats "like a toad" at Eve's ear until the guardian angels Ithuriel (touching him with his spear) and Zephon force him back into his true shape.

q: In the preface to 'Samson Agonistes' ('Of That Sort of Dramatic Poem Which Is Called Tragedy'), Milton cites which philosopher's definition of tragic Catharsis ("to purge the mind of pity and fear")?
e: Milton explicitly invokes Aristotle's 'Poetics' on Catharsis, compares tragedy to homeopathic medicine ("things of melancholic hue and quality are used against melancholy"), and notes that 'Samson Agonistes' was "never intended for the stage" (closet drama).

q: What is the concluding line of Milton's 'Lycidas' (line 193), spoken by the narrator (the "uncouth swain") as he rises at sunset?
o: "Weep no more, woeful shepherds, weep no more."
"To-morrow to fresh woods, and pastures new."
"Fame is no plant that grows on mortal soil."
"Yet once more, O ye laurels, and once more."
e: The final ottava rima stanza (lines 186–193) shifts to third-person narration and closes with the famous line "At last he rose, and twitch'd his mantle blue: / To-morrow to fresh woods, and pastures new." (Note: "woods", NOT "fields"!)

q: Which posthumously discovered Latin theological treatise by Milton (published 1825) revealed his unorthodox Arian (anti-Trinitarian) and mortalist religious views?
e: Discovered in the State Paper Office in 1823 and translated/published in 1825, 'De Doctrina Christiana' revealed Milton's unorthodox beliefs (Arianism — Son subordinate to Father; Mortalism; and tolerance of polygamy), illuminating subtle theology in 'Paradise Lost'.

q: Who remarked on Milton's 'Paradise Lost' in 1674, "This man cuts us all out, and the ancients too," and later adapted 'Paradise Lost' into the rhymed opera 'The State of Innocence'?
e: John Dryden visited the aged blind Milton to ask permission to "tag his verses" (put 'Paradise Lost' into rhyme), to which Milton wryly consented ("Ay, you may tag my verses if you will"). Dryden also praised Milton in his famous 1688 epigram ("Three poets, in three distant ages born...").

q: How many times does Milton invoke the Heavenly Muse directly in 'Paradise Lost', and in which four Books do these invocations occur?
o: Four times — Books I, III, VII, and IX
Three times — Books I, V, and XII
Four times — Books I, II, VI, and X
Two times — Books I and XII
e: Milton's four great personal invocations/proems appear at the openings of Book I (Heavenly Muse), Book III ("Hail, holy Light" — lamenting his blindness), Book VII ("Descend from Heav'n, Urania" — halfway mark), and Book IX (shifting notes to tragic).

q: Which 20th-century critic initially attacked Milton's style in 'Milton I' (1936) for causing a "dissociation of sensibility," before softening his stance in 'Milton II' (1947)?
e: T.S. Eliot criticized Milton's "Chinese Wall" of Latinate syntax and "dissociation of sensibility" in 1936 (echoed by F.R. Leavis's claim of "Milton's dislodgement"), then recanted in 'Milton II' (1947), acknowledging Milton as a great master. C.S. Lewis defended Milton in 'A Preface to Paradise Lost' (1942).

q: Which Miltonic sonnet (Sonnet 7), written upon turning 23 in December 1631, laments that "How soon hath Time, the subtle thief of youth, / Stol'n on his wing my three-and-twentieth year"?
o: On His Having Arrived at the Age of Twenty-Three
When the Assault Was Intended to the City
To Mr. Cyriack Skinner upon His Blindness
e: Sonnet 7 ('How soon hath Time') expresses Milton's anxiety over his "late spring" showing "no bud or blossom," concluding with faith in living "As ever in my great Task-Master's eye."

q: In 'Samson Agonistes', what is the name of the boastful Philistine giant of Gath who comes to mock the blind Samson and retreats in cowardice when Samson challenges him?
e: Harapha of Gath (an invented character, father of Goliath) taunts Samson in the fourth episode, testing Samson's restored faith in God's strength before the Philistine Officer summons Samson to Dagon's festival.

q: What was the title of Milton's 1660 desperate last-minute political pamphlet warning England against restoring the Stuart monarchy on the eve of Charles II's return?
o: The Tenure of Kings and Magistrates
The Readie and Easie Way to Establish a Free Commonwealth
e: Published in February–April 1660 at great personal peril just weeks before Charles II's Restoration (May 1660), 'The Readie and Easie Way' proposed a perpetual Grand Council instead of returning to royal "bondage."

q: In Book X of 'Paradise Lost', who builds the massive causeway ("a bridge of wondrous length") across Chaos linking Hell directly to the newly fallen Earth?
e: Sensing Satan's triumph over mankind, Sin and Death construct a broad paved highway across the abyss of Chaos from Hell's gates straight to the outer shell of the Earth, enabling demons to travel easily to the human world.

q: What was John Milton's FIRST published English poem (printed anonymously in the Second Folio of Shakespeare in 1632)?
o: On the Morning of Christ's Nativity
On Shakespeare ("What needs my Shakespeare for his honour'd bones")
e: Written in 1630 and printed anonymously in the 1632 Second Folio of Shakespeare, 'On Shakespeare' (16 lines in heroic couplets) was Milton's very first poem to appear in print, praising Shakespeare as having built himself "a live-long monument" in readers' hearts.
